## Selection Regret in Credit-Risk Model Updating Under Distribution Shift: The Role of Recent Labeled Information {#selection-regret}

This study examines how the size of a recent labeled sample affects the predictive consequences of selecting a credit-risk model update. It distinguishes the frequency of selecting an oracle policy from the loss incurred when another policy is selected.

::: {.finding}
**Principal findings**

Mean selection regret was lower with 10,000 labeled observations than with 2,500 in all 13 simulation scenarios. Under stability, agreement with the fitted-candidate oracle decreased from 27.6% to 23.6%, while mean selection regret fell by approximately 76.7%. Selecting the oracle policy more often and reducing the cost of selection errors are therefore distinct outcomes.
:::

<details class="methods"><summary>Study design & methods</summary>

The simulation comprises 19,500 replications across 39 conditions, with 500 replications per condition. Stratified five-fold cross-validation selects among four logistic policies using the Brier score: retaining the original model, intercept recalibration, intercept-and-slope recalibration, and full refitting. Evaluation uses a fitted-candidate oracle and a Brier-risk regret decomposition.

A historical Fannie Mae application complements the simulation, with 200 replications at each of three adaptation sample sizes. Larger adaptation samples increased selection success and reduced conditional mean regret in that application.

</details>

## Predictive Stability and Adaptation Under Distribution Shift: Calibration, Discrimination, and Decision Thresholds in Credit-Risk Modeling {#distribution-shift}

<p class="authors">Silas Bambil and Shudeshna Nandy</p>

Discrimination and calibration describe different aspects of predictive performance. This study examines how distribution shift affects probability calibration, discrimination, probability accuracy, and decisions based on predicted risk.

::: {.finding}
**What the study shows**

The relative performance of updating strategies depends on the shift mechanism. Intercept recalibration can accommodate changes in baseline risk, whereas changes in predictor effects may favor refitting. Decision-threshold revision and probability recalibration address different targets.
:::

<details class="methods"><summary>Study design & methods</summary>

The study combines a loan-default benchmark with controlled Monte Carlo experiments. Scenarios include covariate shift with model misspecification, baseline-risk changes, and changes in predictor effects.

Comparisons include retaining the original model, intercept-only recalibration, intercept-and-slope recalibration, importance-weighted refitting, and full deployment refitting. Threshold revision is evaluated separately, with independent data used for final performance assessment.

</details>

<div class="tags"><span>Logistic regression</span><span>Calibration</span><span>Monte Carlo</span><span>Credit risk</span></div>

## Stable Fire-Loss Quantiles and Far-Tail Expected Shortfall Gaps {#fire-loss}

<p class="authors">Silas Bambil</p>

This study analyzes approximately 1.25 million positive-loss records from U.S. structure fires in the 2016–2025 NFIRS releases. Extreme value methods are used to assess severe-loss distributions, high quantiles, and uncertainty in Expected Shortfall.

::: {.finding}
**What the study shows**

High-loss quantiles showed comparatively limited variation across selected modeling choices, whereas Expected Shortfall was more sensitive to tail assumptions and exceptional observations. The results indicate that quantile agreement alone does not establish agreement in expected losses.
:::

<details class="methods"><summary>Data, modeling & robustness</summary>

Peaks-Over-Threshold methods and Generalized Pareto models are used to estimate Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall. Robustness checks include threshold sensitivity, parametric bootstrap, annual tail estimation, leave-one-year-out analysis, event-level aggregation, goodness-of-fit diagnostics, and competing tail models.

</details>

<div class="tags"><span>Extreme value theory</span><span>Tail risk</span><span>Bootstrap</span><span>NFIRS</span></div>

## In development {#in-development}

::: {.planned-study}
<span class="badge planned">Planned follow-up study</span>

### Allocating Deployment Labels Between Model Updating and Intervention Selection Under Distribution Shift

How should a fixed labeling budget be divided between updating a model and selecting an updating intervention? Planned comparisons include all-label refitting, fixed fitting–validation splits, cross-fitting, and adaptive allocation, with final evaluation on untouched test data.
:::
